note: Curated non-AI dichotomous-key dataset for CO / Rocky Mountain prospecting. Property values are standard mineralogy references. hardness is [minMohs, maxMohs]. streak/heft/magnetic are single values; luster/color are lists. target_tags map to engine targets for the soft region bias. Optional 'hazard' flags toxic minerals (arsenic, lead) — always surfaced, even when the ID is uncertain.

minerals.name: Native gold
field_tests: Malleable: dents/flattens with a pin, never shatters (pyrite & mica are brittle and crumble).
Streak stays bright gold (pyrite streaks greenish-black).
Very heavy — pans to the bottom; noticeably heavier than fool's gold.
Color unchanged in shade (pyrite/mica lose their 'gold' look out of direct sun).
minerals.note: The real thing. Soft, dense, malleable, and gold in any light — the opposite of brittle, lighter pyrite/mica.

minerals.name: Pyrite
field_tests: Streak test: greenish-black to brownish-black (gold streaks gold; hematite streaks red-brown).
Hard — H≈6, scratches glass; gold and galena are soft (a knife scratches them).
Brittle: shatters/crumbles under a hammer (gold flattens).
Often in crisp cubes with striated faces.
minerals.note: Classic 'fool's gold': brassy and metallic, but hard, brittle, and it leaves a dark green-black streak.

minerals.name: Chalcopyrite
field_tests: Softer than pyrite (H≈3.5–4): a knife scratches it; pyrite (H6) resists.
Often tarnishes to iridescent blue/purple/green ('peacock' colors).
Streak greenish-black.
minerals.note: A copper-iron sulfide — brassier and softer than pyrite, frequently with peacock tarnish.

minerals.name: Galena
field_tests: Breaks into perfect little cubes (cubic cleavage) — diagnostic.
Surprisingly heavy for its size (lead); very_heavy.
Soft: H≈2.5, a knife scratches it easily.
Bright silver-gray on a fresh break, dulls to gray.
minerals.hazard: Lead mineral — wash hands after handling, don't grind or breathe the dust, and keep it away from food.
minerals.note: Lead sulfide, often silver-bearing. The perfect cubic cleavage + heavy heft + softness are the tell.

minerals.name: Hematite
field_tests: Streak test: RED-BROWN streak is diagnostic — even on a silvery/black 'specular' piece (pyrite = greenish-black; magnetite = black).
Not magnetic (or barely) — magnetite is strongly magnetic.
Often reddish and found with/around iron sulfides like pyrite (oxidation product).
minerals.note: Iron oxide. The classic 'red mineral found with pyrite'. Whatever the surface color, it always leaves a red-brown streak.

minerals.name: Magnetite
field_tests: Strongly magnetic — a magnet grabs it (diagnostic vs hematite/other black minerals).
Black streak (hematite = red-brown).
Common as heavy black sand in a gold pan.
minerals.note: Iron oxide, strongly magnetic. The heavy black sand in your pan — a pathfinder, not a target.

minerals.name: Quartz
minerals.habit: six-sided prisms with pointed ends, conchoidal fracture
field_tests: Hard: H7, scratches glass and steel; won't be scratched by a knife.
No cleavage — breaks with curved (conchoidal) surfaces.
Glassy luster; six-sided crystals ending in a point.
The common host for gold veins — worth checking quartz float.
minerals.note: The most common vein/gangue mineral and a gold host. Glassy, very hard, six-sided crystals, no cleavage.

minerals.name: Muscovite mica
field_tests: Peels into thin, flexible, transparent sheets (diagnostic).
Very soft (H≈2.5) and light.
Flakes glitter gold in the sun in a creek ('fool's gold') but crumble to powder and are weightless — real gold flattens and sinks.
minerals.note: The other 'fool's gold' — glittery flakes in streams. Splits into springy sheets; far too light and brittle to be gold.

minerals.name: Biotite mica
field_tests: Peels into thin flexible sheets like muscovite, but dark brown/black.
Very soft (H≈2.5–3), light.
minerals.note: Dark mica; common in granite and pegmatite. Splits into flexible sheets.

minerals.name: Feldspar
field_tests: Two cleavage directions meeting near a right angle — flat, step-like reflective faces (quartz has none).
Hard (H6): scratches glass but is scratched by quartz.
Green variety (amazonite) is a pegmatite indicator.
minerals.note: The most abundant crustal mineral. Blocky with flat cleavage faces; green amazonite flags pegmatites.

minerals.name: Fluorite
field_tests: Softer than glass (H4): a knife scratches it; won't scratch glass.
Often cubic crystals but cleaves into octahedra (triangular faces).
Vivid purple/green/blue; may glow (fluoresce) under UV.
minerals.note: Colorful and soft. Cubes that cleave to octahedra; too soft to scratch glass (separates it from quartz/beryl).

minerals.name: Beryl
field_tests: Very hard (H≈7.5–8): scratches quartz.
Six-sided prisms, often blue-green (aquamarine); pegmatite gem.
Harder and usually flatter-topped than quartz points.
minerals.note: Pegmatite gem (aquamarine/emerald). Six-sided like quartz but harder and typically blue-green.

minerals.name: Topaz
field_tests: Extremely hard (H8): scratches quartz and beryl.
One perfect cleavage direction (basal).
Often colorless, pale blue, or sherry-yellow; a pegmatite gem.
minerals.note: Very hard pegmatite gem; a single perfect cleavage sets it apart from beryl/quartz.

minerals.name: Corundum
field_tests: Hardness 9 — scratches everything but diamond; nothing common scratches it.
Dense for a gem; barrel-shaped hexagonal crystals.
Red = ruby, blue = sapphire.
minerals.note: Ruby/sapphire. Second only to diamond in hardness — a scratch test against quartz/topaz is decisive.

minerals.name: Garnet
field_tests: Well-formed many-sided (dodecahedral) crystals, no cleavage.
Hard (H≈7): scratches glass.
Deep red-brown; common in metamorphic rock and as a heavy-mineral in pans.
minerals.note: Common metamorphic gem mineral; rounded many-faced crystals, glassy, hard, usually red.

minerals.name: Sphalerite
field_tests: Resinous/greasy luster (looks like hardened tree sap) — distinctive.
Pale yellow-brown streak.
Soft (H≈3.5–4); often with galena in silver-lead-zinc ore.
minerals.note: Zinc sulfide, a silver-ore companion to galena. Resinous luster + yellow-brown streak are the tells.

minerals.name: Barite
field_tests: Surprisingly heavy for a pale, non-metallic mineral (barium) — the giveaway.
Soft (H≈3): a knife scratches it.
Tabular/bladed crystals; a gangue mineral in many veins.
minerals.note: A white/clear mineral that is oddly heavy — that heft on a non-metallic is diagnostic.

minerals.name: Calcite
field_tests: Fizzes in dilute acid (a drop of vinegar bubbles) — diagnostic.
Soft (H3): a knife scratches it easily.
Cleaves into rhombs (leaning cubes); clear pieces double an image.
minerals.note: Common vein/gangue carbonate. The acid fizz + rhombic cleavage are unmistakable.

minerals.name: Rhodochrosite
field_tests: Rose-pink to red; soft (H≈3.5–4).
Rhombohedral cleavage; may fizz weakly in warm acid.
Colorado's state mineral — famous from Sweet Home Mine near Alma.
minerals.note: Pink manganese carbonate — a Colorado specialty, found with silver-lead ores.

minerals.name: Cuprite
field_tests: Deep red, often with green malachite or native copper nearby.
Brownish-red streak (hematite = red-brown too, but cuprite is heavier and sits with copper minerals).
Soft-ish (H≈3.5–4).
minerals.note: A red copper oxide. Like hematite it's red, but it travels with copper minerals (malachite/azurite) not iron sulfides.

minerals.name: Realgar
minerals.hazard: ARSENIC — toxic. Don't lick or taste it, don't breathe the dust, wash hands after handling, and don't carry it loose with food/water. Realgar also crumbles to a toxic yellow-orange powder in sunlight, so store it in the dark.
field_tests: Bright red to orange-red, VERY soft (H1.5–2 — a copper penny scratches it).
Resinous/greasy luster; orange-red streak (hematite streaks red-brown and is far harder).
Medium heft — much lighter than cinnabar (mercury), which is very heavy.
Classically sits WITH pyrite and yellow orpiment in low-temperature / hot-spring veins.
SAFETY: arsenic mineral — handle minimally, wash hands, don't inhale dust.
minerals.note: Bright-red arsenic sulfide, soft and resinous, found with pyrite. Arsenic is a known gold pathfinder — but it's TOXIC, so handle with care.

minerals.name: Orpiment
minerals.hazard: ARSENIC — toxic. Same care as realgar: no tasting, avoid the dust, wash hands after handling.
field_tests: Lemon to golden-yellow, very soft (H1.5–2), pearly/resinous; peels into flexible flakes.
Pale yellow streak.
Realgar's constant yellow companion; found with realgar + pyrite.
SAFETY: arsenic mineral — handle minimally.
minerals.note: Golden-yellow arsenic sulfide, realgar's twin. Toxic (arsenic).

minerals.name: Cinnabar
minerals.hazard: MERCURY — toxic. Never heat it (releases mercury vapor), don't breathe the dust, wash hands after handling, and keep it away from food. Handle sealed if possible.
field_tests: Bright red / vermilion with a red (scarlet) streak — diagnostic.
VERY heavy for its size (mercury) — the heft separates it from realgar (medium) and hematite.
Soft (H2–2.5); adamantine (diamond-like) sparkle on fresh crystals, dull when earthy.
Found in hot-spring / low-temperature veins with pyrite, realgar, and quartz.
SAFETY: mercury mineral — don't heat, don't inhale dust, wash hands.
minerals.note: Red mercury sulfide. Like realgar it's red and sits with pyrite, but it's much heavier (mercury) and softer-streaking scarlet. TOXIC (mercury).

minerals.name: Malachite
field_tests: Bright green; green streak (diagnostic).
Often banded/botryoidal crusts; a copper indicator.
May fizz in acid (a carbonate).
minerals.note: Green copper carbonate — a reliable 'copper is here' pathfinder, often with blue azurite.

minerals.name: Azurite
field_tests: Deep azure blue with a blue streak (diagnostic).
A copper indicator; usually alongside green malachite.
minerals.note: Blue copper carbonate; pairs with malachite as a copper pathfinder.

minerals.name: Native silver
field_tests: Malleable (dents, doesn't shatter) and very heavy; tarnishes dark.
Bright silver-white on a fresh scratch.
Often wiry/dendritic; found with galena/acanthite.
minerals.note: Rare native metal — soft, dense, malleable, tarnishes black. Distinguished from galena by no cubic cleavage.

minerals.name: Molybdenite
field_tests: Extremely soft (H1–1.5) and greasy — marks paper like a pencil.
Bluish silver-gray; leaves a greenish-gray streak (graphite = gray-black).
Colorado's Climax/Henderson are world molybdenum mines.
minerals.note: Molybdenum ore. Looks like graphite but with a bluer, greenish-gray streak; greasy, very soft, flexible flakes.

minerals.name: Graphite
field_tests: Very soft, greasy, marks paper (pencil 'lead').
Gray-black streak; lighter than molybdenite and grayer.
Light for a dark metallic-looking mineral.
minerals.note: Soft, greasy carbon. Distinguished from molybdenite by a gray-black (not greenish) streak and lighter heft.

minerals.name: Limonite / goethite
field_tests: Yellow-brown streak (hematite = red-brown; both are rusty iron oxides).
Dull/earthy rusty crusts — the orange-brown 'gossan' capping oxidized sulfides.
A pathfinder: rusty limonite often marks where pyrite/other sulfides weathered.
minerals.note: Rusty iron-oxide weathering crust. A gossan of limonite over a vein is a classic 'dig here' sign of oxidized sulfides.

minerals.name: Chalcocite
field_tests: Dark lead-gray, soft (H≈2.5–3); a knife cuts it and it's slightly sectile.
A rich copper ore; often with malachite/azurite staining.
Gray-black streak.
minerals.note: A dark-gray copper sulfide ore; soft and sectile, usually with green/blue copper stains.

minerals.name: Arsenopyrite
minerals.hazard: ARSENIC — toxic. Don't lick or taste it, don't breathe the dust, wash hands after handling, and don't carry it loose with food/water.
field_tests: Silvery-white to steel-gray metallic, HARDER than most sulfides (H5.5–6, scratches glass; pyrite is similar but brassier, galena is soft).
Struck sharply with steel it can smell like garlic (arsenic) — diagnostic.
Black streak.
A prime GOLD pathfinder in lode veins — arsenic minerals often ride with gold.
SAFETY: arsenic mineral — handle minimally, wash hands, don't inhale dust.
minerals.note: Silver-gray arsenic-iron sulfide, harder than pyrite. A classic gold pathfinder — but TOXIC (arsenic), so handle with care.

minerals.name: Stibnite
minerals.habit: long striated blades, radiating sprays, often bent
minerals.hazard: Antimony mineral — wash hands after handling, avoid breathing the dust, and keep it away from food.
field_tests: Long silvery-gray blades with lengthwise striations, often bent or radiating (diagnostic).
Very soft (H2) — a knife cuts it, a fingernail nearly scratches it.
Lead-gray streak; metallic.
Forms in low-temperature veins, sometimes with gold and quartz.
SAFETY: antimony mineral — handle minimally, wash hands.
minerals.note: Soft silvery-gray antimony sulfide in bladed sprays. A low-temperature vein mineral that can accompany gold.

minerals.name: Bornite
field_tests: A fresh surface is coppery bronze, but it quickly tarnishes to iridescent purple-blue 'peacock' colors (diagnostic).
Soft (H3): a knife scratches it.
Gray-black streak; a rich copper ore.
minerals.note: 'Peacock ore' — a copper-iron sulfide that tarnishes to vivid purple-blue. Softer and more colorful than pyrite/chalcopyrite.

minerals.name: Pyrrhotite
field_tests: Bronze-brown metallic and WEAKLY magnetic — a magnet tugs it, unusual for a sulfide (but weaker than magnetite, which snaps to the magnet).
Softer than pyrite (H≈4): a knife scratches it.
Gray-black streak.
minerals.note: The 'magnetic sulfide' — bronze iron sulfide that a magnet weakly tugs. Between pyrite and magnetite in both hardness and magnetism.

minerals.name: Cassiterite
field_tests: Very heavy for a non-metallic (SG≈7) — it concentrates in a pan like gold's heavy company.
Hard (H6–7): scratches glass.
Brown to black with a bright adamantine (near-gemmy) luster; near-white streak.
A tin mineral of pegmatites, greisens, and placers.
minerals.note: Tin oxide — brown-black, glassy, and surprisingly heavy. A placer heavy-mineral that travels with tin-bearing pegmatites.

minerals.name: Scheelite
field_tests: Pale (white/tan/amber) but surprisingly heavy (SG≈6) — the weight on a light-colored mineral is the tell.
Glows bright blue-white under short-wave UV (diagnostic).
Moderate hardness (H≈4.5–5): a knife just scratches it.
minerals.note: A pale, heavy tungsten mineral that fluoresces blue-white under UV — the classic way tungsten prospectors find it in the dark.

minerals.name: Wolframite
field_tests: Heavy (SG≈7), dark brown to black with a submetallic luster and one perfect cleavage.
Reddish-brown to brownish-black streak.
Moderate hardness (H≈4–4.5).
A tungsten ore of quartz veins and greisens (Colorado's Boulder County tungsten belt).
minerals.note: Dark, heavy tungsten ore with one perfect cleavage. Far heavier and darker than most minerals of similar hardness.

minerals.name: Cerussite
minerals.hazard: Lead mineral — wash hands after handling, don't grind or breathe the dust, and keep it away from food.
field_tests: White or gray but VERY heavy (lead) with a brilliant adamantine luster — the heft on a pale mineral is the giveaway.
Soft (H3–3.5): a knife scratches it.
Fizzes in warm dilute acid (a carbonate).
Forms as an oxidation crust on galena.
SAFETY: lead mineral — handle minimally, wash hands.
minerals.note: Lead carbonate — the heavy, brilliant white crust that forms as galena weathers. Often silver-bearing. TOXIC (lead).

minerals.name: Native copper
field_tests: Reddish metal, MALLEABLE (dents and bends, never shatters) and very heavy — like gold and silver, it's a native metal.
A fresh scratch is bright copper-red; the surface tarnishes brown, then green.
Often with malachite, azurite, or red cuprite nearby.
minerals.note: Native copper metal — soft, dense, malleable, reddish. Distinguished from copper sulfides by its metal (bendable, not brittle) behavior.

minerals.name: Chrysocolla
field_tests: Sky-blue to blue-green, waxy and often porous/light.
Soft and variable (H2–4): a knife scratches it easily; much softer than turquoise (H5–6).
A copper stain mineral — usually with malachite/azurite; white streak.
minerals.note: A soft blue-green copper mineral. Looks like turquoise but is much softer and lighter — a copper indicator, not a target.

minerals.name: Turquoise
field_tests: Robin's-egg blue to green, waxy luster.
Harder than chrysocolla (H5–6): it resists a knife where chrysocolla doesn't.
A copper phosphate from arid, oxidized copper zones; white streak.
minerals.note: The blue-green gem copper mineral. Harder and denser than look-alike chrysocolla; forms in dry, weathered copper country.

minerals.name: Tourmaline
field_tests: Slender prisms with LENGTHWISE striations and a rounded-triangular cross-section (diagnostic).
Hard (H7+): scratches glass; no cleavage.
Black (schorl) is the common pegmatite type; pink/green/blue are the gem varieties.
minerals.note: A hard pegmatite mineral in striated three-sided prisms. Black schorl is a pegmatite indicator; colored kinds are gems.

minerals.name: Rhodonite
minerals.habit: massive, tabular; often veined with black
field_tests: Rose-pink like rhodochrosite but MUCH harder (H6 — scratches glass; rhodochrosite is soft, H4).
Does NOT fizz in acid (rhodochrosite, a carbonate, may fizz).
Often laced with black manganese-oxide veinlets.
minerals.note: Pink manganese silicate — the hard, non-fizzing look-alike of pink rhodochrosite. The hardness + acid test separate them.

minerals.name: Epidote
field_tests: Distinctive yellow-green 'pistachio' color (diagnostic).
Hard (H6–7): scratches glass.
Slender striated prisms; common in altered and metamorphic rock.
minerals.note: The pistachio-green metamorphic mineral. Its yellow-green color plus hardness set it apart from softer green copper minerals.

minerals.name: Apatite
field_tests: Six-sided prisms like beryl but SOFTER — H5, a knife scratches it and it barely marks glass (beryl H8 scratches quartz).
Green, blue, brown, or yellow; glassy.
It's the '5' on the Mohs hardness scale — a handy reference mineral.
minerals.note: The soft hexagonal-prism mineral — a beryl look-alike that a knife scratches. Marks the middle (H5) of the hardness scale.

minerals.name: Zircon
minerals.habit: stubby square (tetragonal) prisms with pyramid ends
field_tests: Small, hard (H7.5) prisms with a square cross-section and pyramid-capped ends (diagnostic).
Heavy with a brilliant adamantine luster.
A tough heavy-mineral in sands; often slightly radioactive — a pathfinder near radiometric anomalies.
minerals.note: Hard, heavy, square-prism accessory mineral. Its durability makes it a placer heavy-mineral, and it flags radiometric zones.

minerals.name: Native sulfur
field_tests: Bright lemon-yellow, very soft (H2) and light; resinous.
Smells of struck matches; crumbles easily.
Forms around volcanic and hot-spring vents — NOT the same as yellow orpiment (which is an arsenic mineral and heavier).
minerals.note: Bright-yellow native element. Distinguished from toxic yellow orpiment by its lightness, match smell, and volcanic/hot-spring setting.

minerals.name: Gypsum
minerals.habit: clear 'selenite' blades, fibrous 'satin spar', sugary masses
field_tests: Soft enough to scratch with a fingernail (H2) — the '2' on the Mohs scale.
Clear blades (selenite), silky fibers (satin spar), or sugary white masses (alabaster).
Does NOT fizz in acid (separates it from soft, fizzing calcite).
minerals.note: The very soft, fingernail-scratchable sulfate. Comes as clear selenite, silky satin spar, or white alabaster; no acid fizz.

minerals.name: Talc
field_tests: The SOFTEST mineral (H1) — a fingernail scratches it and it feels greasy/soapy.
Pale green to white; non-metallic (unlike greasy graphite/molybdenite, which are dark and metallic).
White streak.
minerals.note: The softest mineral — greasy, soapy, pale. Its non-metallic look separates it from the other greasy softies, graphite and molybdenite.

minerals.name: Serpentine
minerals.hazard: Fibrous (chrysotile) varieties can be ASBESTOS — do not saw, crush, or breathe dust from silky/fibrous pieces. Handle massive pieces only; keep fibrous ones sealed.
field_tests: Mottled green with a greasy/waxy feel; variable hardness (H3–5).
Smooth massive rock (soapstone-like) — but silky FIBROUS veinlets may be asbestos.
White streak.
SAFETY: don't crush or inhale dust from fibrous varieties.
minerals.note: Greasy green metamorphic rock-mineral. Massive kinds are harmless, but fibrous chrysotile is asbestos — don't grind fibrous pieces.

minerals.name: Chalcedony
field_tests: Hard (H7 — it's microcrystalline quartz): scratches glass; a knife won't scratch it.
Waxy to glassy; no cleavage, breaks with curved (conchoidal) surfaces.
Banded = agate; solid red/brown opaque = jasper; translucent = common chalcedony.
minerals.note: Microcrystalline quartz — agate, jasper, chert. Quartz-hard and cleavage-free, but waxy and fine-grained rather than glassy crystals.
